## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Avāriyajātaka* (Ja 376) is a tale preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. In the frame story, the Buddha tells the tale while residing at Jetavana about an ignorant, rough, and hasty ferryman who failed to recognize the qualities of the Three Jewels [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The central moral demonstrates that not everyone can profit from sound counsel, a lesson realized by an ascetic at his own cost [Winternitz 1933].
In the past narrative, the ferryman is known as the father of a daughter named Avāriya (Avāriyapitā) [Fausböll 1883]. Operating his boat across the Ganges, he foolishly transports travelers across the river before requesting his fare, leading to constant quarrels, beatings, and poverty rather than gain [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the characters of the past birth: the foolish ferryman was the same ferryman of the present, King Ānanda was the ruler of that time, and the Bodhisatta was the ascetic [Fausböll 1883].
Textual reuse analysis by DharmaNexus records 17 matching segments between the text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports any early cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
